name: Working Holiday Visa
description: The H-1 Working Holiday visa allows young people aged 18-30 from partner countries to live, work, and travel in Korea for up to one year. It's designed for cultural exchange and short-term work experiences, combining travel opportunities with the chance to earn money along the way.
tagline: Work, travel, and experience Korea for a year
keyRequirement: Citizenship from an eligible country + age 18-30
targetAudience: Cultural explorers wanting to experience Korean life
Backpackers looking to work while traveling Asia

eligibility.label: Age 18-30 at time of application
eligibility.description: Must be between 18 and 30 years old (some countries allow up to 35)

eligibility.label: Citizen of a Working Holiday partner country
eligibility.description: Australia, Canada, France, Germany, UK, Ireland, Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and many others have agreements with Korea

eligibility.label: No accompanying dependents
eligibility.description: You cannot bring family members on this visa

eligibility.label: First-time H-1 applicant (in most cases)
eligibility.description: Most countries only allow one Working Holiday visa to Korea per lifetime

eligibility.label: Good physical and mental health
eligibility.description: Must be in good health with no serious medical conditions

eligibility.label: Sufficient funds for initial stay
eligibility.description: Approximately $3,000+ USD or equivalent to support yourself initially

eligibility.label: Valid travel/health insurance
eligibility.description: Must cover entire duration of stay including medical and repatriation

fees.notes: Fee may vary by country and embassy. Some countries have reciprocal fee waivers.

documents.name: Valid Passport
documents.description: Must be valid for at least 18 months from the date of application

documents.name: Visa Application Form
documents.description: Completed visa application form from Korean embassy/consulate
documents.where_to_get: Download from your local Korean embassy website or obtain at the embassy

documents.name: Passport Photo
documents.description: 3.5cm x 4.5cm, taken within last 6 months, white background

documents.name: Activity Plan / Travel Itinerary
documents.description: Detailed plan of your intended activities, travels, and work intentions during your stay. THIS IS THE MOST CRITICAL DOCUMENT - many applications are rejected due to Seoul-only plans.
tips: CRITICAL: Must include regional/rural destinations - Seoul-only plans are frequently REJECTED
Include specific cities outside Seoul: Busan, Andong (Hahoe Folk Village), Jeonju (hanok village, bibimbap), Gyeongju (ancient capital), Jeju Island
Mention seasonal festivals you plan to attend: Boryeong Mud Festival (July), Jinju Lantern Festival (October), Hwacheon Ice Festival (January)
Show genuine interest in Korean culture: temple stays, traditional craft workshops, Korean cooking classes
Include countryside experiences: staying at a hanok guesthouse, visiting a tea plantation in Boseong, hiking at Seoraksan
Balance work intentions (teaching English, working at hostels, ski resorts) with cultural exploration
Write 1-2 pages minimum with month-by-month breakdown if possible

documents.name: Bank Statement
documents.description: Proof of sufficient funds to support yourself during initial months in Korea
tips: Minimum $3,000 USD recommended (some embassies require more)
Statement should be recent (within 1 month)
Should show consistent balance, not just a recent large deposit

documents.name: Travel/Health Insurance Certificate
documents.description: Proof of comprehensive health insurance covering your entire stay
tips: Must cover medical expenses, hospitalization, and repatriation
Coverage for entire 12-month period
Some embassies require minimum coverage amounts (check your embassy)
Consider Korean NHIS enrollment after arrival for additional coverage

documents.name: Proof of Accommodation (숙소제공확인서)
documents.description: Document showing where you will stay upon arrival in Korea. This is one of the most challenging documents to obtain.
tips: COMMON PROBLEM: Airbnb hosts often refuse to sign accommodation confirmation forms
WORKAROUND: Book a Goshiwon (고시원) for your first month - they are accustomed to signing these forms for visa applicants
Goshiwon costs ₩300,000-500,000/month and provides a small private room, often with shared facilities
Alternative: Some hostels will provide accommodation confirmation if you book an extended stay
The form must include the host's signature, address, phone number, and duration of stay
Some embassies accept hotel reservations for the first few weeks instead

documents.name: Round-trip Flight Reservation
documents.description: Flight itinerary or booking showing return/onward travel
tips: Some embassies only require proof of sufficient funds for return ticket
Booking confirmation is usually sufficient (doesn't need to be fully paid)
Check your specific embassy requirements

documents.name: Resume/CV
tips: Keep it concise (1-2 pages)
Include any relevant experience: teaching, hospitality, languages

documents.name: Criminal Background Check
documents.description: Police clearance certificate from your home country
tips: Processing time varies by country (2-8 weeks)
May need to be apostilled or authenticated
Some embassies don't require this - check your local embassy

applicationSteps.title: Check Eligibility & Gather Documents
applicationSteps.description: Verify your country has a Working Holiday agreement with Korea and that you meet all eligibility requirements. Start collecting required documents.
tips: Check your embassy website for country-specific requirements
Criminal background check can take the longest - start early
Prepare your Activity Plan carefully - this is often why applications fail

applicationSteps.title: Write Your Activity Plan
applicationSteps.description: Create a detailed travel and activity itinerary. This is the most important document for your application.
tips: DO NOT write a Seoul-only plan - this is a common rejection reason
Include at least 3-4 regional destinations outside of Seoul
Mention specific cultural sites: Gyeongbokgung, Bulguksa Temple, Hahoe Folk Village
Include seasonal activities: cherry blossom viewing (April), autumn foliage at Naejangsan (November)
Show interest in rural Korea: Boseong tea fields, Damyang bamboo forest, Suncheon Bay wetlands
Balance work plans with travel and cultural activities

applicationSteps.title: Secure Accommodation Confirmation
applicationSteps.description: Obtain a signed accommodation confirmation from your first place of stay in Korea.
tips: If Airbnb hosts refuse to sign, use a Goshiwon instead
Contact Goshiwons directly - many are experienced with visa paperwork
Popular Goshiwon areas: Hongdae, Sinchon, near universities
Keep the receipt/confirmation for potential immigration checks later

applicationSteps.title: Book Embassy Appointment
applicationSteps.description: Schedule an appointment at your nearest Korean embassy or consulate.
tips: Some embassies allow walk-ins, others require appointments
Peak season (spring/summer) may have longer wait times
Check if your embassy accepts mailed applications

applicationSteps.title: Submit Application
applicationSteps.description: Visit the embassy with all documents. Submit your application and pay the visa fee.
tips: Bring originals AND photocopies of all documents
Dress neatly and be prepared for a brief interview
Have answers ready about your travel plans and intentions

applicationSteps.title: Wait for Processing
applicationSteps.description: Your application will be reviewed. You may be contacted for additional documents or an interview.

applicationSteps.title: Collect Your Visa
applicationSteps.description: Pick up your passport with the visa sticker, or receive it by mail.

applicationSteps.title: Enter Korea & Register for ARC
applicationSteps.description: After arriving in Korea, register for your Alien Registration Card (ARC) at your local immigration office within 90 days.
tips: Book immigration appointment via HiKorea as soon as you arrive
Bring passport, accommodation proof, and application fee
You'll need the ARC to open a bank account and get a phone plan

processingTime.notes: Processing time varies by embassy and season. Summer applications may take longer due to higher volume.

restrictions: Initially limited to 20 hours per week (part-time only)
Cannot work as professional athletes or entertainers
Cannot work as language instructors at official hagwons without additional permit
Can apply for full-time work permit (시간제취업허가) at immigration office
workPermission.notes: After arriving and registering, you can apply for permission to work full-time (40 hours/week) at your local immigration office. Many H-1 holders work at cafes, restaurants, hostels, English tutoring, ski resorts (winter), or farms (seasonal). Remote work for overseas employers is a gray area - technically allowed as it's not Korean employment.

faqs.question: Why was my application rejected for having a Seoul-only Activity Plan?
faqs.answer: Korean immigration wants to see that Working Holiday participants will experience Korea's diverse regions, not just stay in the capital. Include specific plans to visit Busan, Gyeongju, Jeonju, Andong, Jeju Island, or other regional destinations. Mention cultural festivals, rural experiences, and nature activities outside Seoul.

faqs.question: How do I get accommodation proof when Airbnb hosts won't sign the form?
faqs.answer: This is a very common problem. The most reliable workaround is to book a Goshiwon (고시원) for your first month. Goshiwons are small private rooms (often with shared kitchen/bathroom) that cost ₩300,000-500,000/month. They're experienced with visa paperwork and will readily sign the accommodation confirmation form. You can move out after you arrive and find other accommodation.

faqs.question: Can I work full-time on an H-1 visa?
faqs.answer: Initially, you're limited to 20 hours per week. However, after registering for your ARC in Korea, you can visit your local immigration office and apply for a full-time work permit (시간제취업허가). This allows you to work up to 40 hours per week. Bring your passport, ARC, and a letter from your employer.

faqs.question: Can I do remote work for my home country employer on an H-1 visa?
faqs.answer: This is a gray area in Korean immigration law. Technically, remote work for a foreign employer isn't 'employment in Korea' and many H-1 holders do freelance or remote work. However, this isn't explicitly permitted, so maintain a low profile and don't make it your primary stated activity. Focus your Activity Plan on travel and cultural exchange.

faqs.question: How soon should I register for an ARC after arriving?
faqs.answer: You must register within 90 days of arrival, but it's best to do it within the first 2-3 weeks. You'll need the ARC to open a Korean bank account, get a phone plan, and work legally. Book your appointment on HiKorea as soon as you arrive - popular offices can have 2-3 week wait times.

faqs.question: Can I extend my H-1 visa beyond one year?
faqs.answer: No, the H-1 Working Holiday visa cannot be extended. It's strictly limited to one year. If you want to stay longer, you'll need to change to a different visa type (like D-10 for job seeking, D-4 for language study, or get sponsored for an E-7 work visa). Start planning your next steps around month 9 of your stay.

faqs.question: What seasonal jobs are popular for H-1 visa holders?
faqs.answer: Popular seasonal work includes: ski resort jobs in winter (November-March), English tutoring year-round, working at hostels/guesthouses, cafe and restaurant jobs, farm work during harvest seasons, and teaching at English camps during school breaks. Ski resorts in particular often hire H-1 holders and provide accommodation.

faqs.question: Do I need to speak Korean to find work?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, but it helps enormously. Jobs at international hostels, English teaching, and some cafe/restaurant jobs in expat areas (Itaewon, Hongdae) may not require Korean. However, for most jobs, basic Korean will significantly expand your options and improve your experience. Consider taking Korean classes during your stay.

faqs.question: Can I apply for the H-1 visa more than once?
faqs.answer: In most cases, no. The Working Holiday visa is typically a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity per country agreement. However, some countries may have different rules, so check with your local Korean embassy. If you've used your H-1 eligibility, consider other visa options like D-10 (job seeking) or D-4 (language study) for future visits.

tips: Write a diverse Activity Plan - mention at least 3-4 regions outside Seoul, including places like Andong, Jeonju, Gyeongju, Busan, and Jeju
Include seasonal festivals in your plan: Boryeong Mud Festival, Jinju Lantern Festival, Hwacheon Ice Fishing Festival, cherry blossom seasons
For accommodation proof, book a Goshiwon if Airbnb hosts won't sign - they're used to helping visa applicants
Apply in fall or winter for faster processing - spring/summer is peak season with longer wait times
Get your criminal background check early - it can take 2-8 weeks depending on your country
Join Facebook groups for H-1 visa holders in Korea - great for job leads and advice
Consider ski resort work in winter - many provide accommodation and are H-1 friendly
Register for your ARC immediately after arrival - you'll need it for banking and phone plans
Apply for full-time work permit at immigration if you find steady employment
Start planning your next visa around month 9 if you want to stay beyond one year
warnings: DO NOT submit an Activity Plan that only mentions Seoul - this is a common rejection reason
Do not overstay your visa - it will result in fines, deportation, and future visa bans
Do not work more than 20 hours/week without obtaining the full-time work permit
Do not work in prohibited industries (entertainment, adult services)
Always carry your ARC card after you receive it - police can ask for ID
Do not make remote work your primary stated activity in your application
Do not wait until the last minute to register for your ARC - book the appointment early
